name: Pituitary gland
func: A pea-sized gland under the brain, often called the master gland. It releases hormones that control growth, the thyroid, the stress response and how much water your kidneys keep.

levels.kid:
The **pituitary gland** is tiny, about the size of a **pea**, and it hangs under your brain like a little cherry on a stem. It sits safely in a cozy bony cup in the middle of your head.

Even though it is small, it is the **boss** of lots of other glands, so people call it the **master gland**. It sends chemical messages called **hormones** through your blood.

One hormone helps you **grow** taller. Others tell your neck gland to keep your energy up and help your body handle **stress**. Another one tells your kidneys to save water when you are thirsty, so you don't dry out.
levels.hs:
The **pituitary gland** (hypophysis) is about 1 cm across and sits in the **sella turcica** ("Turkish saddle"), a hollow in the **sphenoid bone** at the center of the skull base. It hangs from the **hypothalamus** by the **pituitary stalk** (infundibulum). Directly above it is the **optic chiasm**, and on each side is a **cavernous sinus** containing the internal carotid artery and several cranial nerves. Below it is the **sphenoid sinus**.

It has two parts with different origins:
- The **anterior pituitary** (adenohypophysis) is true gland tissue. It makes **growth hormone (GH)**, **thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)**, **adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)**, which tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol, and **prolactin**, another pituitary hormone, among others.
- The **posterior pituitary** (neurohypophysis) is really part of the brain. It stores and releases **antidiuretic hormone (ADH)**, also called vasopressin, which is made in the hypothalamus and tells the kidneys to hold on to water.

The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary with **releasing hormones** delivered through a tiny private blood system, and the target glands send **negative feedback** to keep levels balanced.
levels.college:
**Development**: the anterior lobe grows up from the roof of the embryonic mouth as **Rathke's pouch**, while the posterior lobe grows down from the floor of the diencephalon. Remnants of Rathke's pouch can form **Rathke's cleft cysts** and **craniopharyngiomas**.

**Blood supply and portal system**: the **superior hypophyseal arteries** (from the internal carotid) form a primary capillary bed in the **median eminence**, where hypothalamic neurons release hormones such as **GHRH**, **somatostatin**, **TRH**, **CRH** and **dopamine**. **Long portal veins** carry these down the stalk to a second capillary bed in the anterior lobe. The **inferior hypophyseal arteries** supply the posterior lobe. Pituitary venous blood drains into the cavernous sinuses.

**Anterior lobe cells** include **somatotrophs** (GH, the most numerous, about half), **corticotrophs** (ACTH, from the precursor **POMC**), **thyrotrophs** (TSH) and **lactotrophs**, with others. Lactotrophs are unusual: they are mainly under **inhibitory** control by hypothalamic **dopamine**, so cutting the stalk raises this hormone while the others fall.

**Posterior lobe**: magnocellular neurons of the **supraoptic** and **paraventricular** nuclei send axons down the stalk (the **hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract**) and release **ADH** from swollen terminals (Herring bodies) directly into blood. ADH acts on **V2 receptors** in the kidney collecting ducts to insert **aquaporin-2** water channels.

The **diaphragma sellae**, a fold of dura, roofs the sella; the stalk passes through its central opening.
levels.phd:
Pituitary hormone release is pulsatile and network-driven. Endocrine cells are linked into 3D **homotypic networks** (Mollard and colleagues showed GH cells connected by adherens and gap junctions) that coordinate pulses and can remodel with physiological demand. **GH secretion** is driven by alternating hypothalamic **GHRH** and **somatostatin** rhythms, with large pulses during **slow-wave sleep**; the stomach hormone **ghrelin** also stimulates GH via the GHS-R1a receptor.

The **HPA axis**: CRH and vasopressin from parvocellular PVN neurons act synergistically on corticotrophs (CRHR1 and V1b receptors) to release ACTH, cleaved from **POMC** by prohormone convertase 1/3. Cortisol feeds back on glucocorticoid receptors in the pituitary, hypothalamus and hippocampus. The axis shows a **circadian rhythm** (peak early morning) entrained by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, and ultradian pulses about hourly.

**Osmoregulation**: osmoreceptors in the **OVLT** and subfornical organ (circumventricular organs lacking a blood–brain barrier) sense plasma tonicity; magnocellular neurons fire phasic bursts that release ADH. A rise of only around 1–2% in plasma osmolality is enough to trigger release, and thirst is coupled to the same sensors.

Pituitary development depends on transcription factors **PROP1**, **POU1F1 (PIT-1)**, **HESX1** and **TBX19 (TPIT)**; mutations cause combined pituitary hormone deficiencies. Adult pituitary stem cells marked by **SOX2** can regenerate some cell types. Somatotroph adenomas often carry activating **GNAS** mutations (the gsp oncogene), and corticotroph adenomas frequently carry **USP8** mutations that stabilize the EGF receptor.
levels.expert:
**Pituitary adenomas** (now often called pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, PitNETs) are among the most common intracranial tumors. Microadenomas are under 1 cm; macroadenomas are 1 cm or more. They cause trouble in two ways: **mass effect** (headache, **bitemporal hemianopia** from chiasmal compression, hypopituitarism, and cavernous sinus invasion graded by the **Knosp** scale) and **hormone excess**:
- **GH excess**: **acromegaly** in adults (enlarging hands and feet, coarse face, jaw growth, sleep apnea, heart disease) or **gigantism** before growth plates close. Screened with **IGF-1** and confirmed by failure of GH to suppress during a glucose tolerance test.
- **ACTH excess**: **Cushing disease** (central obesity, purple striae, muscle weakness, high blood pressure and glucose).
- Secreting tumors of the pituitary hormone controlled by dopamine are usually treated first with **dopamine agonist** medication rather than surgery.

**Posterior pituitary / hypothalamic damage** causes **arginine vasopressin deficiency** (formerly central diabetes insipidus): large volumes of dilute urine, thirst and high serum sodium (above 145 mmol/L). After pituitary surgery, sodium is watched closely for a **triphasic response**.

**Pituitary apoplexy** (sudden hemorrhage or infarction of an adenoma) presents with thunderclap headache, vision loss, eye movement palsies and possible acute adrenal crisis; urgent steroid replacement is needed and sometimes urgent decompression.

**MRI with dynamic contrast** is the key imaging. Most operations use an **endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal** approach through the nose and sphenoid sinus, with care to protect the carotid arteries and avoid **CSF leaks**. **Craniopharyngiomas** in children, often calcified and cystic, are challenging because they stick to the hypothalamus.

keyPoints: Pea-sized gland in the sella turcica, below the optic chiasm, between the cavernous sinuses
Anterior lobe (gland, from Rathke's pouch) vs posterior lobe (neural tissue)
Anterior: GH, TSH, ACTH and others; posterior releases ADH made in the hypothalamus
Hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the anterior lobe through the portal system
Adenomas cause hormone excess (acromegaly, Cushing disease) and bitemporal hemianopia

test.q: The pituitary gland sits in a hollow of which bone?
test.explain: The sella turcica is a saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone.

test.q: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the ______ pituitary.
test.explain: Magnocellular neurons send axons down the stalk and release ADH in the posterior lobe.

test.q: An adult with growing hands and feet and a coarsening face most likely has excess:
test.explain: GH excess after growth plates close causes acromegaly; IGF-1 is the screening test.

choices: Rathke's pouch (roof of the embryonic mouth)
test.explain: The posterior lobe comes from the diencephalon; the anterior from Rathke's pouch.

test.q: Pituitary tumors are usually removed through the nose by the ______ approach.
test.explain: The endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal approach reaches the sella through the sphenoid sinus.
